title: "Computation time of survival fits"

Multilevel unanchored meta-regression (ML-UMR) compares a treatment for which
individual patient data are available from a single-arm study with a
comparator for which only aggregate evidence is published, adjusting for
differences between the covariate distributions of the two populations
[@ChandlerIshakMLUMR]. In its extension to time-to-event outcomes
[@ChandlerIshak2026], the likelihood of the comparator evidence is integrated
over the covariate distribution of the comparator population, which multiplies
the number of likelihood terms by the number of integration points. The cost
of evaluating the log posterior density, and hence the duration of a fit, is
therefore dominated by the comparator likelihood.

The `mlumr()` argument `optimization` controls computational optimizations:
changes to the way in which the log posterior density and its gradient are
evaluated that leave the statistical model, and therefore the posterior
distribution, unchanged. This article documents the optimization introduced in
version 0.2.1, the per-arm reuse of the comparator linear predictor in the
survival models (hereafter *predictor reuse*), and reports a simulation study
of its effect on computation time.

## The `optimization` argument

Optimizations are enabled by default and are disabled with
`optimization = FALSE`:


``` r
# Predictor reuse (the default).
fit <- mlumr(dat, distribution = "weibull")
# The arithmetic of releases before 0.2.1.
fit_ref <- mlumr(dat, distribution = "weibull", optimization = FALSE)
```

The setting is stored in the fitted object as `fit$model_controls$optimization`,
and `prior_sensitivity()` refits the model with the same setting. In the
present release the argument affects the survival family only; it has no
effect for binary, continuous, or count outcomes. It is unrelated to Stan's
optimization algorithms: the posterior distribution is always explored by
Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling.

Disabling optimizations serves two purposes: benchmarking, as in the study
reported below, and repeating the arithmetic of releases before 0.2.1, so that
a fit obtained with such a release can be reproduced exactly when the Stan
version, the compiler, and the seed are also the same.

## The modified computation

In a survival fit the comparator evidence consists of reconstructed
pseudo-individual data, and the likelihood of each pseudo-individual is
integrated over the covariate distribution of the comparator population, in
the manner of the population adjustment of multilevel network meta-regression
[@Phillippo2020]. With integration points $x_{a1}, \dots, x_{aM}$ for
comparator arm $a$, the likelihood contribution of pseudo-individual $j$, with
observed time $t_j$ and event indicator $d_j$, is

$$
L_j = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^{M} f\!\left(t_j, d_j \mid \eta_{am}\right),
\qquad
\eta_{am} = \mu_{C} + x_{am}^{\top} \beta,
$$

where $f$ is the density or survival function of the chosen distribution,
$\mu_C$ is the comparator intercept, and $\beta$ is the vector of comparator
covariate coefficients. The linear predictors $\eta_{a1}, \dots, \eta_{aM}$
depend on the arm and on the parameters but not on $j$. Releases before 0.2.1
nevertheless recomputed them for every pseudo-individual: one product of the
$M \times n_B$ design matrix with the coefficient vector per pseudo-individual
and per evaluation of the log density, where $n_B$ is the number of design
columns. With predictor reuse they are computed once per arm and evaluation and
shared by all pseudo-individuals in the arm.

Stan evaluates the gradient of the log density by reverse-mode automatic
differentiation [@Carpenter2017], and the No-U-Turn sampler [@Hoffman2014]
evaluates this gradient at every leapfrog step. Each matrix-vector product
creates $M$ new values in the expression graph, together with the bookkeeping
needed to differentiate them, and in the reverse pass propagates $M$ adjoints
into $n_B$ coefficients. Predictor reuse removes all but one product
per arm. It leaves unchanged the $n_{\text{agd}} \times M$ likelihood terms
$f$, the likelihood of the index study, and the priors. The relative reduction
per evaluation therefore equals the share of the total cost that is
attributable to the removed products. It is expected to be larger when the
design is wider (more covariates, or the relaxed model with its separate
comparator coefficients) and the likelihood terms are inexpensive, and smaller
when the likelihood terms or the index study dominate the cost.

Both computations evaluate the same function. The matrix-vector products yield
identical values, but the reverse pass accumulates the contributions to each
coefficient's gradient in a different order: once per arm after summation over
pseudo-individuals, rather than once per pseudo-individual. Because
floating-point addition is not associative, the two gradients may differ in
their final digits. The posterior distribution is identical; under a common
seed the draws coincide until such differences accumulate along the sampler's
trajectory, which can happen as early as warmup, and they agree in
distribution throughout. The package's parity tests (`tests/parity/` in the
source repository) compare, for each of 52 test cases and both settings, the log density, its gradient, the parameter
transforms, and every generated quantity against the 0.2.0 models.

## Simulation study design

The design is reported following the ADEMP structure of @Morris2019: aims,
data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods, and performance measures. The
estimands are computational rather than statistical: the study measures
computation time and verifies numerical agreement, rather than bias or
coverage.

The study was implemented in the script
[`data-raw/simulate_survival_performance.R`](https://github.com/choxos/mlumr/blob/main/data-raw/simulate_survival_performance.R),
which is part of the package source repository but is not installed with the
package. The script writes, alongside its results, a manifest that records the
software and hardware used. The results reported below were computed from
files with MD5 digests cdf8546e6f7a093f725259a8dac61d22 (per-evaluation timings) and
654dc369f68c9d2007a96f62d21dfa81 (complete fits); a package test verifies these digests against
the files in the repository.

### Aims

1. **A1.** To estimate the reduction in time per evaluation of the log density
   and its gradient, the operation repeated at every leapfrog step of the
   sampler, and its dependence on the fitted distribution, the model, the
   number of comparator pseudo-individuals $n_{\text{agd}}$, the number of
   integration points $M$, and the number of covariates $K$.
2. **A2.** To estimate the part of that reduction that carries over to a
   complete `mlumr()` fit.
3. **A3.** To verify that the computations with and without predictor reuse,
   and the 0.2.0 models, produced the same values in every run of the study.

### Data-generating mechanism

A single data-generating mechanism was used throughout, as a benchmark
design. Computation time depends mainly on the code path of the fitted model
and on the sample sizes. It also depends on the data values: through the mix
of event and censoring indicators, through branches of the generalized gamma
likelihood that are selected by the values of time and of the parameters, and,
in complete fits, through the trajectories of the sampler. The study does not
vary these sources systematically.

* An index study of 200 individuals and a comparator cohort of
  $n_{\text{agd}}$ individuals were generated in the same way.
* The $K$ covariates alternated between continuous (normal, SD 1) and binary.
  The comparator population was shifted by 0.2 on the continuous covariates and
  had prevalence 0.45, against 0.5 in the index population, on the binary
  covariates.
* Event times followed a Weibull proportional hazards model with shape 1.2,
  coefficients 0.3, -0.2, 0.15, -0.1, 0.25, and -0.15 (the first $K$ of
  these), a baseline median of approximately five months, and a conditional
  log hazard ratio of -0.4 for the index treatment.
* Censoring times were independent and exponentially distributed with rate
  0.02 per month, with administrative censoring at 24 months: right censoring
  only, without delayed entry.
* The comparator cohort's times and event indicators were supplied to
  `set_agd_surv()` as its pseudo-individual data, together with its realized
  covariate means, standard deviations, and proportions. For the purposes of
  computation this is equivalent to a digitized Kaplan-Meier curve.
* Integration points were generated by `add_integration()` with its default
  Gaussian copula. The restricted mean survival time (RMST) was computed to
  18 months, and predictions were made at 6, 12, and 18 months.

Each data set was shared by every fitted distribution and model of the same
size, so that these comparisons were made on the same individuals.

### Methods compared

* **With predictor reuse** (`optimization = TRUE`): the 0.2.1 survival models,
  which compute the linear predictor once per comparator arm.
* **Without predictor reuse** (`optimization = FALSE`): the same compiled
  models, which recompute the linear predictor for every pseudo-individual.
* **Version 0.2.0**: the survival models as released in mlumr 0.2.0, retained
  unchanged in the repository for the parity tests. This comparison addresses
  two further questions: whether version 0.2.1 is faster than the previous
  release, and whether the switch between the two computations adds any cost
  when predictor reuse is disabled.

### Level A: time per evaluation

**Workloads.** The workloads comprised every combination of fitted
distribution (Weibull, log-normal, generalized gamma, and the M-spline flexible
baseline), model (SPFA and relaxed), $n_{\text{agd}}$ (100, 500, 2000), $M$
(16, 64, 256), and $K$ (1, 3, 6): 216 workloads, each with two
data sets. The piecewise exponential baseline shares the likelihood code of
the M-spline baseline and was not measured separately.

**Measurement.** Time was measured inside the CmdStan executable used by
`mlumr(engine = "cmdstanr")`, through CmdStan's `log_prob` method, which reads
a file of parameter values and, for each row, evaluates the log density and
its gradient and writes the result. The CPU time of a run over $N$ rows minus
the median CPU time of three runs over five rows, divided by $N - 5$,
estimates the cost per row with process start-up, data input, and model
construction removed. The three short runs were made once for each data set
and method, so all blocks of a data set share this subtraction. The cost per
row comprises one evaluation of the log density and its gradient together
with reading one row of parameter values and writing one row of results. The
reading and writing are the same for the three methods; they dilute the
relative reductions slightly for the least expensive workloads without
favoring any method. $N$ was chosen for each data set so that a run lasted
approximately 0.5 s, subject to a minimum of 20 rows, and was the
same for all three methods. The minimum applied to
17% of runs, and the longest run took
6.1 s of CPU time.

**Parameter values.** The parameter values were five draws from CmdStan's
Laplace approximation at the posterior mode of each data set, so that timings
were taken in the region of the parameter space explored by the sampler.
For 67 of the 432 data sets (57 generalized gamma and 10 Weibull) the posterior mode could not be located, and the origin together with four small perturbations of it was used instead.

**Pairing.** Each data set was timed in eight blocks, and within a
block each of the three methods was run once. The orders of the methods in the
eight blocks were the six possible orders, each used once, and two
further orders that both began with predictor reuse, assigned to blocks at
random. Predictor reuse therefore ran first in four of the
eight blocks of every data set, and each of the other methods in
two; every method occupied every
position. The effect of this imbalance was estimated in a sensitivity
analysis. Data sets were processed in random order, so that any temporal drift
in timing was distributed across the experimental factors.

**Estimand and uncertainty.** For each block, the estimand was the log ratio
of the time per evaluation without predictor reuse to the time with it, and
likewise for the 0.2.0 models. Because the blocks of a data set share the
subtracted cost of the short runs, the data set rather than the block was
taken as the independent unit. The estimate for a workload was the mean of its
two data-set means, each the mean of eight block log ratios. With two
data sets per workload, the variance between data-set means cannot be
estimated reliably for each workload separately. It was therefore pooled over
the 18 workloads that share the distribution and the number
of integration points. Because the two models of a given size were fitted to
the same data sets, these workloads comprise 9 independent
pairs of data sets, and the 95% interval for a workload used the $t$
distribution with 9 degrees of freedom. In a sensitivity
analysis, a linear model for the log time with effects of block, method, and
position within the block was fitted to each workload, giving estimates
adjusted for position. Results are reported as the percentage reduction in
time per evaluation, $100\,(1 - 1/\text{ratio})$.

### Level B: complete fits

**Scenarios.** Two SPFA scenarios with three covariates and 64 integration
points were studied: a Weibull baseline with 500 comparator pseudo-individuals
(ten data sets) and an M-spline baseline with 300 (five data sets). The smaller
number of M-spline data sets, which reflects the longer run time of these fits,
was fixed before any fit was run.

**Fits.** Each data set was fitted with `optimization = TRUE` and with
`optimization = FALSE` through `mlumr(engine = "cmdstanr")` with the default
sampler settings (four chains of 2000 iterations, of which 1000 were warmup,
`adapt_delta = 0.95`, `max_treedepth = 15`). The four chains ran in parallel,
and both fits used the same seed and hence the same initial values. The order
of the two settings alternated between data sets. Draws were written with 18
significant digits. A chain was regarded as following a common trajectory
under both settings when, at every sampling iteration, each sampled parameter
(the regression coefficients and the auxiliary and spline parameters) differed
between the settings by at most $10^{-6} \max(1, |x|)$, where $x$ is its
value with predictor reuse. This tolerance admits the rounding differences
described above but not a separation of trajectories.

**Estimands.** The primary estimand was the sampling time per leapfrog step,
paired by data set and chain. It is dominated by the cost of a step within the
actual sampler. Because the sampling time also includes work done once per
iteration (the generated quantities and the writing of draws), it is not
entirely independent of the number of steps per iteration, but it is much less
sensitive to that number than the elapsed time is. The secondary estimands were the elapsed time of the `mlumr()` call and
the bulk effective sample size (ESS) of the comparator-population RMST
difference per second of elapsed time. Each was summarized as the mean of the
log ratios over data sets, with a $t$ interval; with five or ten data sets
these intervals are necessarily wide.

0.2.0.9000 is the development version of 0.2.1. Level A ran one
CmdStan process at a time; Level B ran the four chains of each fit in
parallel. A unit of either level was started only when the one-minute load
average was below 6. The load average was recorded
immediately after each timed run in Level A, with median
4.7 (range
3.3 to 9.5),
and at the start of each fit in Level B, with median
5.7 (range
3.4 to 10.6).
Because the one-minute load average decays over about a minute, the recorded
values include the unit's own preceding runs as well as other activity on the
machine, and the two contributions cannot be separated.

## Results

### Agreement

Across the 432 data sets of Level A, the largest absolute difference in
the log density or in any component of its gradient between the computations
with and without predictor reuse, over all parameter values timed, was
1.6e-10; between predictor reuse
and the 0.2.0 models it was 1.6e-10.
In every data set the two differences were identical, which is consistent with the computation without predictor reuse and the 0.2.0 models producing identical output.

## Discussion

### Principal findings

**Time per evaluation (A1).** Averaged over the other factors, predictor reuse
reduced the time per evaluation of the log density and its gradient for every
distribution and for both models. The 95% interval excluded no change in
182 of the 216 workloads, and in
none did it indicate an increase.
The reduction was largest for the M-spline baseline
(19.4% on average over the other factors) and smallest for
the generalized gamma distribution (5.2%), whose
likelihood terms evaluate incomplete gamma functions and therefore leave the
removed products a smaller share of the total cost.

The dependence on the other factors agreed with the structure of the
computation. The reduction increased with the number of covariates, from
11.3% with one covariate to 14.3% with six, and was
larger for the relaxed model than for the SPFA model (13.4%
against 12.2%), since both widen the design. It increased
slightly with the number of pseudo-individuals, from 11.4% at
100 to 13.6% at 2000, as the fixed cost of the index study's
likelihood became a smaller share of the total. It decreased with the number
of integration points, from 16.2% at 16 to 11.2%
at 64 and 10.8% at 256. The operation count does not predict
this dependence, because both the removed products and the likelihood terms
grow linearly with $M$. A decrease followed by a plateau is consistent with a
cost per product that does not grow with $M$, such as the bookkeeping needed
to differentiate each product, which is a larger share of the total when $M$
is small.

The reductions relative to the 0.2.0 models were close to those relative to
the computation without predictor reuse, because the two took nearly the same
time: averaged over workloads, the 0.2.0 models took
0.5% longer than the computation without
predictor reuse (95% interval 0.1% to
0.8%, computed over the 27
data-set sizes). The data flag that selects between
the two computations therefore did not slow the computation without predictor
reuse.

**Complete fits (A2).** In the Weibull scenario predictor reuse reduced the
sampling time per leapfrog step by 8.6% (95% interval 2.2% to 14.7%), in
agreement with the Level A estimate of
10.1% (95% interval 5.9% to 14.1%) for the same distribution,
model, sample size, number of integration points, and number of covariates.
The elapsed time of the `mlumr()` call was reduced by
7.6% (95% interval 0.5% to 14.1%), and the bulk ESS of the RMST
difference per second increased by a factor of
1.08 (95% interval 1.00 to 1.17).
In the M-spline scenario the point
estimates were larger, a reduction of
17.2% (95% interval -11.0% to 38.3%) per leapfrog step and
27.0% (95% interval -2.9% to 48.2%) in elapsed time, compared with
14.9% (95% interval 11.3% to 18.4%) per evaluation in Level A
at 500 pseudo-individuals. With five data sets these intervals include no
change, and the M-spline estimates are not conclusive. The M-spline estimate
for elapsed time exceeds that per leapfrog step because the fits without
predictor reuse happened to take more leapfrog steps in sampling
(11% more in total)
and a longer warmup (39%
longer in total). Because the chains of the two settings followed different
trajectories, these differences reflect the paths taken by the sampler rather
than an effect of predictor reuse, which is why the time per leapfrog step is
the primary estimand.

**Agreement (A3).** At every parameter value timed, the log density and its
gradient with predictor reuse agreed with those without it, and with those of
the 0.2.0 models, to within
1.6e-10 in
absolute value. In the complete fits,
31 of the
40 Weibull chains and
0 of the
20 M-spline chains followed a common trajectory
under both settings throughout sampling. Of the 29 chains that
separated, 26 had done so by the first sampling iteration,
that is, during warmup. In every pair of fits the posterior means of the RMST
difference differed by at most
0.027 posterior
standard deviations, which is comparable with the Monte Carlo standard error
of a single fit's posterior mean (at most
0.017 posterior standard
deviations).

### Limitations

All timings were obtained on one machine with one compiler, and through
CmdStan (`engine = "cmdstanr"`) only. Absolute times, and to a lesser extent
the relative reductions, depend on the processor, the compiler, and its
optimization flags; the results are not claimed to hold for other hardware or
for the rstan engine.

The two levels measure different quantities. Level A reports the CPU time of a
single process that evaluates the log density and its gradient at fixed
parameter values. Level B reports the elapsed time of complete `mlumr()` calls
whose four chains ran in parallel. This time also includes data preparation,
the generated quantities, reading the sampler output, and post-processing, and
it depends on the number of leapfrog steps that the sampler takes. When the
two settings take the same number of steps, the work that predictor reuse does
not affect dilutes the reduction, and the reduction in elapsed time is
expected to be smaller than the reduction per evaluation. Once trajectories
separate, however, the number of steps differs between the settings by chance,
and the reduction in elapsed time of an individual fit can be larger or
smaller than the reduction per evaluation, as in the M-spline scenario.

The Level A intervals assume that the variance between the data-set means of a
workload is the same for all workloads with the same distribution and number
of integration points. With two data sets per workload this assumption cannot
be checked for each workload, and the pooled estimates for workloads that share
data sets are correlated. The pooled variance includes both the variation
between data sets and the error of the short runs subtracted from all blocks
of a data set. The allocation of orders to blocks was unbalanced, although the
position-adjusted estimates differed little from the primary estimates.

Level B comprised two scenarios with ten and five data sets, and its intervals
are correspondingly wide. The reduction in elapsed time for other
distributions, sample sizes, numbers of integration points, or for the relaxed
model was not measured directly and can be inferred only from the
corresponding Level A workloads.

A single data-generating mechanism was used, with right censoring only.
Delayed entry and left or interval censoring add terms to each likelihood
evaluation and would be expected to reduce the share of the total cost that
predictor reuse removes. For
67 data sets the timings were taken at fallback parameter
values rather than at draws near the posterior mode. The cost of the
incomplete gamma functions in the generalized gamma likelihood depends on the
parameter values, but within workloads the reductions at the two kinds of
points did not differ systematically (see Results). That comparison is between
different data sets; no data set was evaluated at both kinds of points.

Although each unit started only when the load average was below the stated
threshold, the machine was not otherwise idle; the recorded load averages are
reported above. Background activity adds variability to individual timings.
In Level A, the random order of data sets and the allocation of every method
to every position within blocks limit its effect on the comparison. In Level
B, the order of the two fits of a pair may also affect timing; its cause was
not determined. The alternation of the two settings balanced the order exactly
for the Weibull scenario (5 of
10 data sets with predictor reuse first) and
approximately for the M-spline scenario
(3 of
5). Weighting the two orders equally gives
reductions per leapfrog step of
8.6% for the
Weibull scenario and
18.5% for the
M-spline scenario, and reductions in elapsed time of
7.6% and
25.5%.

Finally, the processor has four performance cores and four efficiency cores,
and the assignment of processes to core types was left to the operating
system. A chain scheduled on an efficiency core runs more slowly, which is a
plausible source of the variability between data sets in Level B, where four
chains ran concurrently.

### Conclusion

Predictor reuse removes redundant computation from the survival models without
changing the model, the posterior distribution, or the computed values beyond
the final digits of floating-point sums. In this study it reduced the time per
evaluation of the log density and its gradient by
12.4% in the median workload and by up to
30%, with the largest reductions for the M-spline baseline, wide designs, and few integration points,
and the smallest for the generalized gamma distribution. In complete Weibull
fits, most of whose chains followed a common trajectory under both settings,
the elapsed time was reduced by about
8%. Because the optimization is enabled by
default, these reductions apply to survival fits without any change to user
code; `optimization = FALSE` remains available for benchmarking and for
reproducing fits made with earlier releases.

## Reproducibility

The study can be reproduced from the root of the package source, with that
source installed:


``` r
# Each stage records every completed unit and resumes from there if interrupted.
system("Rscript data-raw/simulate_survival_performance.R fixed")
system("Rscript data-raw/simulate_survival_performance.R fits")
system("Rscript data-raw/simulate_survival_performance.R assemble")
```

The final stage writes the results files and the manifest, which records the
commit of the package source, the software versions, and the machine.
